headline: White Island Ledge Wakes Up: Cod on the Drift, Bass Stacking the Piscataqua
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't sound like much until you've fished the Shoals right — this week the groundfish came back and the bunker pushed the stripers into the rivers.
body_markdown:
People who don't know this coast look at the map and figure thirteen miles isn't worth the trailer wax. Those people have never run out to White Island on a slack tide in September and watched a diamond jig get stopped cold forty feet down. The Isles of Shoals fish like they're offshore because structurally, they basically are — six miles of open water separates Rye Harbor from ledges that hold cod, haddock, and pollock the way spots three times the distance do everywhere else in the Gulf of Maine. This week that structure started paying off again, and the timing lines up with everything else going on inshore.

The new moon on the 10th put a real charge into the tide, and that's the story for both the groundfish and the stripers right now. Out at the Shoals, the harder current on the bigger swings has cod and haddock moving up off bottom to feed on the drift rather than sitting dead still, which makes them easier to find and easier to hook. Boats working the rockpiles around Appledore and White Island Ledge in 60 to 90 feet have been finding cod to eight pounds on diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid or mackerel belly, worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood. Haddock have been mixed in on the same drifts, smaller on average but consistent, and a few pollock showing on the shallower humps closer to Duck Island for boats jigging faster with bare tin.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker schools tightening under the building moon would get the stripers committing for real instead of just picking at stragglers, and that's exactly what's happened in Hampton Harbor and up the Piscataqua. Bunker pods have been getting pinned against the jetties at Hampton on the last of the incoming tide, and bass in the 24 to 34-inch range have been working them hard right at the mouth, particularly on the north side channel edge where the current stacks bait against the rocks. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, three-quarter to one ounce, swum just under the surface through the wash have been drawing strikes, and topwater has worked too in the last hour of daylight when the blitzes get visible from Great Boars Head.

The Piscataqua has been the more consistent bite of the two rivers. Bass are staging at the mouth near Fort Point and working up past Henderson's Point on the push, feeding on the same bunker that's getting squeezed by the current funnel through Portsmouth Harbor. That funnel effect is what makes the river fishery different from the open beach — bait gets trapped and concentrated instead of just passing through, so the window is longer and the fish sit tighter to structure. Live bunker on a fish-finder rig, or a swimming plug worked slow along the current seams on the last of the flood, has been the play. Sizes have been decent, not giant — plenty of low-to-mid-30s fish, with the occasional better one mixed in from boats working the deeper holes right off the bridge pilings.

Bluefish have been the sleeper story. Snapper blues are thick in Hampton Harbor and up in the back channels toward Seabrook, which is the usual tell that bigger blues are close behind as the water keeps cooling. A few adult blues in the four-to-six-pound range have already turned up mixed in with the striper blitzes at the harbor mouth, hitting the same bucktails and metal the bass are eating. That's worth watching over the next week, because once the adults show in numbers they tend to take over the top-water bite entirely and the bass slide underneath them.

Mackerel have pushed in tight to shore as the Gulf of Maine water continues its seasonal cooldown, and that's part of what's fueling the groundfish bite at the Shoals — cod and haddock following forage in instead of holding on the deeper edges. Jigging mackerel off the rockpiles at Odiorne Point and around the outer edge of the Shoals in the early morning has been an easy way to fill a bait bucket before running out to the ledges, and it doesn't hurt to keep a few rigged as fresh strip bait for the cod jigs.

Looking at the next several days, the tide is still carrying real push from Wednesday's new moon, and that should keep both patterns going — bunker staying tight to structure in the rivers and current staying strong enough to work the fish up off the Shoals bottom. If the wind stays out of the northwest and light like it's been, the water should hold clean, which matters more at the Shoals than people think; a dirty tide out there kills visibility on the jig and the bite goes quiet fast. The tidal push will start easing by the weekend as the moon moves away from new phase, so the smart move is fishing the next two or three days hard rather than waiting. For groundfish, target the last two hours of the ebb at White Island and Appledore. For bass, the first hour of the incoming at Hampton Harbor's north jetty and the last of the flood on the Piscataqua near Henderson's Point are the windows worth building a morning around. Keep an eye on the blues — if the adults keep showing in the numbers the snappers suggest, that's the story for the second half of September on this coast.
